ety.text: From Middle English fewe, from Old English fēaw (“few”), from Proto-West Germanic *fau, from Proto-Germanic *fawaz (“few”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”). Cognate with Old Saxon fā (“few”), Old High German fao, fō (“few, little”), Old Norse fár (“few”), Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌿𐍃 (faus, “few”). Also related with Latin paucus (“little, few”) and pauper (“poor”), from which latter English poor and pauper; see these.

senses.d: An indefinite, but usually small, number of.
ex: There are a few cars (=some, but a relatively small number) in the street.
Quite a few people (=a significant number) were pleasantly surprised.

senses.d: Not many; a small (in comparison with another number stated or implied) but somewhat indefinite number of.
ex: Very few did she have not to go there, did she?
I was expecting a big crowd at the party, but very few people (=almost none) turned up.

senses.d: Obscuring one to two oktas (eighths) of the sky.
ex: Tonight: A few clouds. Increasing cloudiness overnight.

senses.d: (US?) Having a 10 percent chance of measurable precipitation (0.01 inch); used interchangeably with isolated.

ex: Many are called, but few are chosen.

grp.label: meteorology: obscuring 1–2 eighths of the sky

ety.text: Inherited from Old French poi, from Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare Catalan poc, Italian poco, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco. Cognate with English few.
From Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ukos, derived from the root *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare French peu, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco.
Inherited from Old Spanish poco, from Latin paucus. Cognate with Catalan poc, French peu, Italian poco, and Portuguese pouco, as well as English few.

phr: a few clowns short of a circus

a few roos loose in the top paddock

few cards shy of a full deck

ety.text: From Middle English fewere, equivalent to few + -er.

senses.d: Less; a smaller amount of something non-integral commonly expressed as an integer
ex: Leaving from my home in Alameda, the heavily BART-assisted journey took fewer than five hours round trip.

grp.label: comparative of few; a smaller number

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish menos, inherited from Latin minus, comparative of parum.
From Old Galician-Portuguese menos, displacing collateral form mẽos, from Latin minus, neuter of minor (“lesser; smaller”), comparative of parvus (“small”).
